# 123 · A cache expiry turned from a boolean into the time left, proved expired exactly when none is left

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✓ Verified: equivalent on every input outside the declared change** | functional, no-false-positive | none | refactor, behaviour change not intended | [`Expiry#remainingNanos`](../../examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/cache/Expiry.java) | [B9: Regression verification](../../lib/README.md) |

> A cache's expire-after-write test returned whether an entry had expired. A developer turns it into the time the entry has left, so that an eviction can be scheduled for the moment it expires and the metrics endpoint can report it, and callers test `<= 0`. A regression proof compares results of one type, and these are a boolean and a long. The developer states how they are related instead, `previous == (result <= 0)`, and the proof is of that relation between the new method and the previous one on every input the cache can pass.

Tags: [caching](../README.md#tag-caching), [clocks-and-time](../README.md#tag-clocks-and-time), [signature-change](../README.md#tag-signature-change)

## The change

Replace `isExpired(writtenAtNanos, ttlNanos, nowNanos)` with `remainingNanos(writtenAtNanos, ttlNanos, nowNanos)`: the time to live less the time since the write, `FOREVER` for an entry that never expires, so that an entry is expired exactly when the result is zero or negative. The four tests and the law in the properties file are rewritten for the time left; the API contract records the new signature.

The developer declares which inputs the change is meant to affect: `!(writtenAtNanos >= 0 && nowNanos >= writtenAtNanos && ttlNanos > 0)`. The verifier proves that every other input behaves as before, or shows one that does not.

The method's signature changed, so the developer states how the previous version is called from the new parameters: `net.terminalvalue.crosscut.cache.Expiry#isExpired()`. The verifier proves that on every input, the new method agrees with the previous one called that way, or shows one on which it does not.

The result changed its type or its meaning, so the developer states how the two results are related, `previous` being the result of `net.terminalvalue.crosscut.cache.Expiry#isExpired` and `result` the new method's: `previous == (result <= 0)`. The verifier proves that the relation holds on every input where both versions return, and that they throw alike where they throw, or shows an input on which they do not.

**Before** ([`Expiry.java`](../../examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/cache/Expiry.java), line 1):

```java
package net.terminalvalue.crosscut.cache;

/**
 * The expire-after-write test of a cache entry, with {@code Long.MAX_VALUE} as the time to live meaning "never", as
 * Caffeine and Spring's cache abstraction treat it. The clock reading is passed in, so that the cache can be
 * driven by a {@code Clock} in tests and by {@code System.nanoTime()} in production.
 */
    // ...

    public static final long FOREVER = Long.MAX_VALUE;

    /** Whether an entry written at {@code writtenAtNanos} with the given time to live has expired at {@code nowNanos}. */
    public static boolean isExpired(long writtenAtNanos, long ttlNanos, long nowNanos) {
        if (ttlNanos == FOREVER) {
            return false;
        }
        return nowNanos - writtenAtNanos >= ttlNanos;
    }
}
```

**After:**

```java
package net.terminalvalue.crosscut.cache;

/**
 * The expire-after-write time left to a cache entry, with {@code Long.MAX_VALUE} as the time to live meaning "never", as
 * Caffeine and Spring's cache abstraction treat it. The clock reading is passed in, so that the cache can be
 * driven by a {@code Clock} in tests and by {@code System.nanoTime()} in production.
 */
    // ...

    public static final long FOREVER = Long.MAX_VALUE;

    /**
     * How long an entry written at {@code writtenAtNanos} with the given time to live has left at {@code nowNanos}: zero or
     * negative once it has expired, {@link #FOREVER} for an entry that never does, so that an eviction can be scheduled for
     * when the entry expires and the cache's metrics can report the time left.
     */
    public static long remainingNanos(long writtenAtNanos, long ttlNanos, long nowNanos) {
        if (ttlNanos == FOREVER) {
            return FOREVER;
        }
        return ttlNanos - (nowNanos - writtenAtNanos);
    }
}
```

## What the verifier found

For every input where `!(writtenAtNanos >= 0 && nowNanos >= writtenAtNanos && ttlNanos > 0)` is false, the new code returns a result related to the old code's by `previous == (result <= 0)`, or throws what it threw.

This is a proof over the whole domain (writtenAtNanos: long × ttlNanos: long × nowNanos: long), not a sample. JBMC turned the statement into a satisfiability problem over the bytecode of both versions and showed that it has no solution: no input exists on which they differ.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

Every existing unit test passes, as it should (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.crosscut.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

A regression proof usually stops here: the harness compares what the two versions return, and a boolean is never equal to a long. Without a proof the rewrite rests on four test cases and a reading of `ttlNanos - (nowNanos - writtenAtNanos)` against `nowNanos - writtenAtNanos >= ttlNanos`. A subtraction the other way round, a sentinel returned as zero, or an entry that lives forever handled after the arithmetic instead of before it would make every entry expire at once or never, and a test suite that checks a second to go, exactly expired and long expired would still pass for the sentinel mistake.

## Why the verdict is right

The developer names the previous method, `previousSymbol`, and states how the results are related, `resultsAgreeWhen`: `previous == (result <= 0)`, a boolean expression over the new parameters, `previous` (the previous version's result, a boolean) and `result` (the new one's, a long). The tool resolves the previous version in the old classes, type-checks the relation against both return types, and compiles it into the harness in place of the equality it would otherwise assert: on every input, both versions must throw alike, and when both return the relation must hold; a relation that throws on a pair of results does not hold. The proof is restricted to the inputs the cache can pass, the precondition the module's own properties file states: a write at or after the clock's zero, read at or after it, with a positive time to live. Outside it the new method's signed subtraction can overflow, for a reading from before the write against a time to live near the maximum, and the relation is not claimed. Within it the relation is proved over all 2^192 inputs in under a second. A counterexample would be shown as both results with the note that the relation does not hold between them; example 122 shows one.

## What to do

Merge. The relation and the precondition are what a reviewer approves: that expired means no time left, and that the cache never asks about a reading from before the write. The identical-bytecode shortcut is off under a relation, since identical code proves nothing about `previous == (result <= 0)`.

## Notes

- The library's test of the same shape (the same `isExpired` turned into `remainingNanos`) proves in 0.4 s with JBMC and in 0.1 s with the tool's own checker; the measurement on this kernel is the pipeline's.
- Without `resultsAgreeWhen`, the tool refuses: `the previous version returns boolean and the new one long; say how the results are related with --results-agree-when, a boolean expression over the new parameters, previous and result`. The relation may also be given when the types are the same and the meaning changed, `result == previous * 1000L` for seconds that became milliseconds.
- The scope is the negation of the precondition in `properties.contract` (`writtenAtNanos >= 0 && nowNanos >= writtenAtNanos && ttlNanos > 0`), so that the proof line reads `where !(!(...))`: the relation holds wherever the module's own property is claimed. Without the scope the proof finds inputs outside it on which `ttlNanos - (nowNanos - writtenAtNanos)` overflows, a clock reading from before the write against a time to live near `Long.MAX_VALUE`, which the old comparison of differences survives; those are the inputs the precondition excludes, not a defect of the rewrite.
- The relation is checked again on a replayed counterexample, in the interpreter, so that a counterexample from a method JBMC had no bytecode for is recognised as one that does not reproduce, as for an equality.

## Evidence

How the verdict was reached: JBMC 6.11.0: 2 properties proved over writtenAtNanos: long × ttlNanos: long × nowNanos: long in 0.3 s; loops unwound 16 times with unwinding assertions.

This result was recorded before runs fingerprinted their inputs, so whether it still matches the current patch and sources is not known.

```java
/** Generated by jvmcontract: asserts that two versions of a method agree. The class file JBMC checks is generated directly; this is the same statement, for readers. */
public final class EquivalenceHarness {
    public static void check(long writtenAtNanos, long ttlNanos, long nowNanos) {
        if (!(writtenAtNanos >= 0 && nowNanos >= writtenAtNanos && ttlNanos > 0)) { return; } // the inputs the developer meant to change
        boolean a = false;
        int ea = 0;
        try { a = before.net.terminalvalue.crosscut.cache.Expiry.isExpired(writtenAtNanos, ttlNanos, nowNanos); } catch (java.lang.NumberFormatException t) { ea = 1; } catch (java.lang.ArithmeticException t) { ea = 2; } catch (java.lang.NullPointerException t) { ea = 3; } catch (java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { ea = 4; } catch (java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { ea = 5; } catch (java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException t) { ea = 6; } catch (java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException t) { ea = 7; } catch (java.lang.ClassCastException t) { ea = 8; } catch (java.lang.IllegalStateException t) { ea = 9; } catch (java.lang.IllegalArgumentException t) { ea = 10; } catch (java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException t) { ea = 11; } catch (java.util.NoSuchElementException t) { ea = 12; } catch (java.util.ConcurrentModificationException t) { ea = 13; } catch (java.lang.RuntimeException t) { ea = 14; } catch (java.lang.Error t) { ea = 15; }
        long b = 0;
        int eb = 0;
        try { b = net.terminalvalue.crosscut.cache.Expiry.remainingNanos(writtenAtNanos, ttlNanos, nowNanos); } catch (java.lang.NumberFormatException t) { eb = 1; } catch (java.lang.ArithmeticException t) { eb = 2; } catch (java.lang.NullPointerException t) { eb = 3; } catch (java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { eb = 4; } catch (java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { eb = 5; } catch (java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException t) { eb = 6; } catch (java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException t) { eb = 7; } catch (java.lang.ClassCastException t) { eb = 8; } catch (java.lang.IllegalStateException t) { eb = 9; } catch (java.lang.IllegalArgumentException t) { eb = 10; } catch (java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException t) { eb = 11; } catch (java.util.NoSuchElementException t) { eb = 12; } catch (java.util.ConcurrentModificationException t) { eb = 13; } catch (java.lang.RuntimeException t) { eb = 14; } catch (java.lang.Error t) { eb = 15; }
        // The results agree when the stated relation holds: previous is the previous version's, result the new one's.
        boolean previous = a; long result = b;
        assert ea == eb && (ea != 0 || (previous == (result <= 0)));
    }
}
```

**Provenance:** Constructed on the expire-after-write kernel of example 033, whose property proof holds the boolean to its law; the rewrite is the time-left form an eviction wheel and a metrics endpoint need. The technique is regression verification under a stated relation between the versions' results.

- [Godlin and Strichman, Regression verification: proving the equivalence of similar programs (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1002/stvr.1472)
- [System.nanoTime (Java SE 21): compare two readings by their difference, never by magnitude](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/System.html#nanoTime())
- [Caffeine: expireAfterWrite and the Expiry interface](https://github.com/ben-manes/caffeine/wiki/Eviction#time-based)
